title: n8n vocabulary, in plain English
promise: You'll learn the fifteen n8n words that show up constantly. Each one explained plainly, with an example from the flow you already have running. You'll stop reading the docs and the forums like they're written in another language.
why: Marcos has been using n8n for two weeks and is making good progress, until something breaks and he goes looking for a fix. The forum answer says: "the trigger isn't emitting items because the webhook is in test mode; use the production URL and check the payload in the execution." Each word on its own rings a bell; the whole sentence is fog. He closes the forum and starts changing things at random. The problem wasn't technical: it was vocabulary. Fifteen words separate someone who can search for solutions from someone who depends on luck.

theory.title: Why a whole lesson for this
theory.text: Vocabulary isn't general knowledge here: it's the diagnostic tool. When something fails, the fix will be written in a forum, in the docs, or an AI will give it to you. In all three cases it'll come in this language. Whoever has it down copies the error, understands the answer, and fixes it in ten minutes. Whoever doesn't rephrases their problem in vague terms ("the email thing isn't working") and gets vague answers back.
theory.analogy: Going to the mechanic knowing how to say "it makes a noise when braking cold" instead of "it does weird stuff." Precise language is half the fix.

theory.title: The words for the drawing: workflow, node, connection
theory.text: The workflow is the whole drawing, your complete automation: one per process. Each box is a node, and it does exactly one thing. The arrows are connections, and they aren't decorative: they define which way the data travels and in what order. When the docs say "add a node after the trigger," they mean "put another box to the right of the trigger and connect it."
theory.example: Your flow from yesterday: a workflow with four nodes and three connections. You've already built it; today you put names to it.

theory.title: The words for movement: item, execution, payload
theory.text: An item is each element that travels over an arrow: an email, a row, an order. An execution is each time the whole flow gets set in motion, and it stays saved with its data. The payload is the content that arrives: when a service sends you a notification, the payload is the data package it carries inside. These are the three words that come up most in any diagnostic conversation.
theory.example: "The 9:00 execution processed 12 items" = the flow started at nine and twelve rows passed through it. "Check the webhook's payload" = open what arrived and read what was inside it.

visual.title: The fifteen, to lock in
visual.caption: Click each card: the word first, the meaning behind it. Go through them until none of them surprise you.

cards.meaning: The whole drawing: your complete automation. One per process.
Each box. Does exactly one thing: watch, decide, transform, or act.
The one that decides WHEN everything starts. Only one per flow.
Each element that travels over an arrow: an email, a row, an order.
Each time the flow runs, saved with its real data.
The data package that arrives inside a notification. What the messenger is carrying.
The saved data n8n uses to log into a service on your behalf.
An address of yours where other services notify you. They call you, not the other way around.
The formula between curly braces that grabs a piece of data from an earlier step: {{ $json.name }}.
Data frozen on a node so you can test without calling the real service every time.
A webhook's two addresses: the test one (only works with the editor open) and the real one.
A separate flow that fires when another one fails. Your alarm system.
A flow that another flow calls, like calling a function. So you don't repeat pieces.
The cap on calls a service accepts per minute. Go over it and you get a 429 error.
Your own n8n, installed by you, as opposed to their cloud. Free, with maintenance on you.

theory.title: The words for the plug: credential, webhook, expression
theory.text: You already know the credential: you created it yesterday, and it's the saved permission to log into a service. A webhook is an address of yours that other services send notifications to. Instead of asking every minute if there's news, they call you. And an expression is the formula between double curly braces that grabs a piece of data from an earlier step. {{ $json.name }} means "the name field of the item that arrives." Expressions get a whole lesson to themselves, lesson 16, because they're the glue holding everything together.
theory.example: In yesterday's email you typed the subject by hand, but you picked the field with the selector: that generated an expression for you. In lesson 16 you'll write them yourself.

theory.title: The two that save you scares: pin and the two URLs
theory.text: Pinned data means freezing a node's data. You run it once and lock in the result. From there you test the rest of the flow without calling the real service again. It saves time, calls, and scares. The webhook's two URLs are the classic trap. The test one only works while the editor is open; the production one, when the flow is activated. Half the "my webhook isn't receiving anything" posts on forums come from having put the test one into the real service.
theory.example: With the sheet's data pinned, you can tweak the filter twenty times without making twenty calls to Google. Unpin it when you're done and you're set.

theory.title: How you use this when something breaks
theory.text: The professional sequence is always the same. Open the failed execution, find the red node, and read its error. Then search or ask using the exact words: "n8n [node] [error message]." With vocabulary, a question to an AI goes from "the email thing isn't working" to "the Gmail node returns 401 in the execution even though the credential is verified." That way, the first answer is usually already the right one.
theory.analogy: The difference between "it hurts around here" and "sharp pain on the right side when I breathe in." Whoever describes it well gets diagnosed fast.

visual.title: The same question, with and without vocabulary
visual.caption: Both describe the same problem. Only one gets a useful answer.

rows.after: "The Gmail node returns 401 on every execution"
"The webhook isn't receiving the payload on the production URL"
"The node runs once per item and I want it once per execution"
"The expression returns undefined because the field has a different name"

visual.gain: The ones on the right get solved on the first answer. The ones on the left spawn three more questions.

tasks.title: Translate your flow from yesterday
tasks.where: With your flow from lesson 06 open
tasks.action: Say it out loud using the new words: how many nodes your workflow has, which one is the trigger, how many items passed through the last execution, and which credential it uses. It sounds like a joke; it's exactly the exercise that locks in the language.
tasks.expect: A sentence of your own like: "my workflow has four nodes, the trigger is a schedule, the last execution moved twelve items, and it uses two credentials."
tasks.stuck: If a word won't come, open the flashcards above and find where that thing is in your real flow.

tasks.title: Try the pin on your sheet
tasks.where: In your flow's Google Sheets node
tasks.action: Run the flow, open the Sheets node, and find the pin icon in its output panel. Turn it on. Now run the flow two more times: you'll see the node stops calling Google and uses the frozen data instead. Unpin it when you're done.
tasks.expect: Two instant runs through the Sheets section, and understanding what it's for: testing without spending calls.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the icon, search "pin data" in your version's help. It's in every version, sometimes with a different icon.

tasks.title: Read a forum sentence and translate it
tasks.action: Translate Marcos's sentence into plain English: "the trigger isn't emitting items because the webhook is in test mode; use the production URL and check the payload in the execution." Write it in your own words.
tasks.expect: Something like: "nothing's firing because the webhook address you gave is the test one, which only works with the editor open; use the real one and check what data arrived in the history."
tasks.stuck: Go word by word with the flashcards. The sentence uses six of the fifteen.

tasks.title: Write your first professional question
tasks.where: In a notes app, as a template for the future
tasks.action: Write out the template you'll use when something fails: "In n8n [where it runs: cloud/self-hosted], the [which] node returns [literal error] in the execution. The item arriving into it carries [fields]. The credential is [status]. What should I check?" Save it next to your notes.
tasks.expect: A three-line template ready to fill in on the bad day.
tasks.stuck: You don't need to memorize it: just knowing it exists and where it is is enough.

tasks.title: Review the flashcards tomorrow
tasks.action: Come back tomorrow for two minutes and go through the fifteen cards once. Vocabulary sticks with two passes separated by a night's sleep, not one long pass.
tasks.expect: Tomorrow, no card surprises you. That's the bar.
tasks.stuck: Any that trip you up two days in a row, write them in your notes: those are the ones you'll misuse most on forums.

errors.message: "Trigger" and "webhook" seem like the same thing to me
errors.means: Almost: the trigger is the category (any box that starts a flow), and a webhook is ONE type of trigger (the one that waits for outside notifications). Yesterday's schedule is another type.
errors.fix: Quick rule: every webhook that starts a flow is a trigger; not every trigger is a webhook. If it starts on a schedule, it's a schedule trigger; if it starts because another service calls in, it's a webhook.

errors.message: I put the webhook URL into the other service and nothing arrives
errors.means: You copied the Test URL, which only works while the editor is open and listening.
errors.fix: Every webhook has two addresses. For it to work on its own, copy the Production URL and activate the flow. The test one is for testing with the editor in front of you. Lesson 27 covers it in detail.

errors.message: I pinned data and now the flow is using old data
errors.means: Pinning freezes it: as long as it's on, that node won't call the real service again, not even when activated.
errors.fix: Unpin the node when you're done testing. Habit: pin it for one testing session and remove it before saving and activating.

errors.message: The docs are in English and I get lost
errors.means: That's the real state of the ecosystem: the good documentation and the forums are all in English, using this vocabulary.
errors.fix: The good news: these fifteen words cover 90% of it. Once you recognize them, the rest translates fine with any translator without losing the meaning. You don't need fluent English: you need these fifteen words.

matters: The three words for movement: item, execution, payload. They show up in every diagnosis, and mixing them up makes you look for the bug in the wrong place.
The webhook's two URLs. Test for trying it out with the editor open, production for it to actually work. Half the forum webhook problems come from this mix-up.
Asking with the literal error and the exact vocabulary. It's the difference between solving it on the first answer and spending the afternoon rephrasing.
The pin, for testing without spending. Every real call to a service costs time and sometimes money; frozen data makes tests instant.
ignore: Advanced administration vocabulary: workers, queues, scaling, custom environment variables. It exists for big installations and isn't yours yet.
Memorizing expression syntax. Today it's enough to recognize {{ }} when you see it; writing them is all of lesson 16.
Enterprise version terms: SSO, RBAC, environments. If you ever need them, you'll have someone next to you to translate.
canDo: Turn you into someone who searches and finds: with these fifteen words, forums and docs go from fog to instructions.
Get you the right answer from an AI on the first try, because your question carries the exact node, error, and context.
Let you test cold with the pin: twenty filter tweaks without twenty calls to Google.
Give you a webhook's two addresses clearly labeled, so you pick the right one.
cantDo: Translate the official documentation for you: it's in English and will stay that way. The fifteen words are the bridge.
Warn you that you left a pin on: the node will keep using frozen data until you remove it yourself.
Guess what your vague question means. "It's not working" can't be diagnosed, not by a forum and not by an AI.
Stop the vocabulary from growing: new words will show up. But with these fifteen, the new ones make sense from context.
words: The whole drawing, your complete automation. One per process.
Decides when everything starts; one per flow.
Each element that travels over an arrow.
Each run, saved with its data.
The data package that arrives inside a notification.
The saved permission to log into a service on your behalf.
Your own address where other services notify you.
The {{ }} formula that grabs data from earlier steps.
Freezing a node's output so you can test without calling the real service.

pieces.title: You've got the vocabulary down if
pieces.caption: Five checks. The last one is the one you'll use in real life.
items: You can describe yesterday's flow using workflow, node, trigger, item, and credential
You can say what tells an execution apart from an item
You can tell the Test URL apart from the Production URL and when each one works
You know what a pin does and why you have to remove it when you're done
You can write a forum question with the node, the literal error, and the context
